name: Pang Lhabsol
when: Late August or September (15th day of the 7th Tibetan month)
summary: Pang Lhabsol honours Mount Khangchendzonga as the guardian deity of Sikkim and remembers the blood-brotherhood oath between the Lepcha and Bhutia peoples. In Gangtok the highlight is the warrior masked dance, Pang Toed Chaam, performed in the courtyard of the palace monastery.
body: The festival is unique to Sikkim. It is said to have been introduced by the third Chogyal, Chakdor Namgyal, in the early 18th century to give thanks to Khangchendzonga and its attendant deities. It also recalls the oath of brotherhood sworn between the Lepcha chief Thekong Tek and the Bhutia leader Khe Bumsa at Kabi Longstok, with the mountain called as witness.

In Gangtok the main event is the Pang Toed Chaam at the Tsuklakhang, the royal chapel near the old palace. Monks dressed as warriors and as Dzonga, the deity of Khangchendzonga, dance with swords and shields to the sound of long horns and cymbals. The Sikkim government declares a state holiday and the town fills with families in their best clothes.

The festival falls in the tail of the monsoon, so expect rain, landslide delays on NH10 and cloud over the peaks. It is a good reason to visit Gangtok in a quiet season, and hotel prices are lower than in October.
tips: Confirm the date each year, as it follows the Tibetan lunar calendar
Arrive early at the Tsuklakhang courtyard for a place to stand
Ask before photographing monks and families, and never use flash during the dance
Allow spare time for monsoon road delays on NH10
Ravangla in South Sikkim holds a larger Pang Lhabsol gathering if you can travel there

faqs.q: When is Pang Lhabsol celebrated in Gangtok?
faqs.a: Pang Lhabsol falls on the 15th day of the seventh month of the Tibetan calendar, which lands in late August or September. The exact date changes every year. Sikkim Tourism and the state holiday list publish it in advance, and hotels in Gangtok can confirm it closer to the time.

faqs.q: Can tourists watch the Pang Lhabsol masked dance?
faqs.a: Yes. The Pang Toed Chaam at the Tsuklakhang in Gangtok is open to the public, and visitors are welcome to watch respectfully from the edges of the courtyard. Dress modestly, keep your voice low, do not walk across the dance area, and ask before taking close photographs of people.

It honours Mount Khangchendzonga as the guardian deity of Sikkim and commemorates the blood-brotherhood treaty between the Lepcha and Bhutia communities, sworn with the mountain as witness. The festival is unique to Sikkim and is said to date from the reign of the third Chogyal, Chakdor Namgyal.

faqs.q: Is late August a good time to visit Gangtok for the festival?
faqs.a: It is a quieter, cheaper time to visit, but it is still the monsoon. Expect rain most days, cloud over the peaks and occasional landslides on NH10 between Siliguri and Gangtok. Build a spare day into your plan, and keep high-altitude trips to Tsomgo flexible in case of road closures.

name: Losoong and the Kagyed Chaam
summary: Losoong is the Sikkimese New Year at the end of the harvest, celebrated mainly by the Bhutia and Lepcha communities. In the days before it, monasteries in and around Gangtok perform the Kagyed Chaam, a masked dance that symbolically destroys the evils of the old year.
body: Losoong, also called Namsoong by the Lepcha, marks the end of the farming year, when barns are full and families gather. The Kagyed Chaam is held on the 28th and 29th days of the tenth Tibetan month at the Tsuklakhang in Gangtok and at other monasteries such as Phodong in North Sikkim. On the final day an effigy representing evil is burnt.

December is cold and clear in Gangtok, with the best mountain views of the year. That makes this a fine time to combine the festival with a Tsomgo trip, though snow may close Nathu La and the Zuluk road on some days. Archery contests and family feasts with local food and chhang, a millet beer, are part of the celebrations.
tips: Dates follow the Tibetan calendar, so confirm them with Sikkim Tourism each year
Dress warmly, as outdoor dances can last several hours in the cold
Book Gangtok rooms early because the festival runs into the Christmas season
Keep a flexible day for Tsomgo in case snow closes the road

faqs.a: The Kagyed Chaam is a masked dance performed by monks just before Losoong. Dancers represent protective deities, and the dance symbolises the destruction of evil and misfortune from the passing year. It ends with the burning of effigies. In Gangtok it is held at the Tsuklakhang, the royal chapel near the old palace.

Losoong usually falls in December, at the end of the tenth month of the Tibetan calendar, after the harvest. The Kagyed Chaam takes place on the 28th and 29th days of that month. Exact dates change every year, so check the Sikkim government holiday list or ask your hotel.

faqs.q: Is December a good month to visit Gangtok?
faqs.a: Yes, for clear skies and mountain views. Days are cool, around 5–15°C, and nights are cold. Snow sometimes closes the road to Nathu La and above Tsomgo for a day or two, and Zuluk can be snowbound. Check current status before you travel and pack warm layers.

The monastery dances are open to respectful visitors. Family feasts and village celebrations are private, but homestay guests are sometimes invited to share food. If you are invited, accept a little of everything offered, and follow your hosts' lead on when to eat and how to sit.

name: Losar at Rumtek
when: February or early March (1st day of the 1st Tibetan month)
summary: Losar is the Tibetan New Year, celebrated across Sikkim by Buddhist communities. Rumtek, the main seat of the Karma Kagyu school in India, marks it with prayers, offerings and masked dances in the days before the new year begins.
body: In the last days of the old year, monasteries perform rituals to clear away obstacles, often including masked dances in honour of the protector Mahakala. At Rumtek these take place in the main courtyard, with monks in brocade and masks moving to drums and long horns. Families visit the monastery in new clothes, light butter lamps and exchange khadas.

The first days of Losar are spent with family, and some shops and restaurants in Gangtok close. February is cold but often clear, and the rhododendrons start flowering at lower altitudes by March. It is a quiet, cheap time to visit, though Tsomgo may still be frozen and Nathu La can close after snow.
tips: Ask the monastery or your hotel for the exact dance dates, which follow the lunar calendar
Carry photo ID, as Rumtek has a security check at the gate
Expect some shops and restaurants to close for the first days of Losar
Dress modestly and walk clockwise around temples and stupas

faqs.q: When is Losar celebrated at Rumtek?
faqs.a: Losar falls on the first day of the first Tibetan month, usually in February or early March. The ceremonies and masked dances at Rumtek take place in the days just before the new year. Dates change every year, so confirm them with the monastery office or a Gangtok travel agent.

faqs.q: Are tourists allowed into Rumtek during Losar?
faqs.a: Yes, visitors are generally welcome to watch the public ceremonies, but the security check at the gate still applies and you need photo ID. Some halls may be closed for private rituals. Keep to the edges of the courtyard, do not use flash, and follow any instructions from monks.

Gangtok stays open, but some family-run shops, restaurants and offices close for the first two or three days of the new year. Hotels, taxis and the main tourist services keep working. It is a good idea to book cars for permit trips in advance during this period.

faqs.q: What is the weather like in Rumtek in February?
faqs.a: February is cold, with daytime temperatures of roughly 8–15°C and frost possible at night. Skies are often clear, giving good views across the valley. Carry warm layers for long outdoor ceremonies. Higher up, Tsomgo Lake is often frozen and the Nathu La road can close after fresh snow.
